intro: The second part of section 34.4 covers Freud's later theory and the work of the analysts who built on it. It starts with the structural model of id, ego and superego from 1923 and the ego functions that ego psychologists describe, then turns to synthetic and autonomous functions, signal anxiety, and the four classes of defense mechanisms in Table 34-12. It ends with the classic theory of neuroses, the core of analytic technique, and the many ways analysts have described transference and its mechanisms, from displacement to projective identification. Update boxes add what later classification did with defenses and neuroses.
objectives: Describe the id, ego, superego and ego-ideal in the structural model, and explain why Freud moved beyond the topographic model.
List the basic ego functions, tell reality testing apart from the sense of reality and from adapting to reality, and give Hartmann's primary and secondary autonomous functions.
Contrast Freud's dammed-up libido theory of anxiety with signal anxiety, and order the danger situations from annihilation to superego anxiety.
Classify defense mechanisms as narcissistic-psychotic, immature, neurotic or mature, and define each defense in Table 34-12.
Summarize the classic psychoanalytic theory of neuroses and Freud's four childhood cases, and define free association, resistance, transference neurosis and countertransference.
Recognize the transference variants and the three transference mechanisms, and explain how later analysts came to use countertransference as information.
